children: Inflation in the Philippines accelerated to a fresh multiyear high in October, justifying the central bank's decision to deliver an oversized interest-rate hike last month.
Consumer-price growth accelerated to 7.8%, the fastest pace since February 2023 and up from September's 7.2%, data from the Philippine Statistics Authority showed Thursday.

Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas had expected inflation to stay elevated last month, forecasting a range of 7.1% to 8.1% due to pressure from fuel, electricity and transport prices. A Wall Street Journal poll of eight economists had put October's print at 7.9%.

The continued inflationary pressure backs the central bank's policy stance. The BSP has been among the most aggressive in tightening policy settings in the wake of the oil crisis caused by war in the Middle East, delivering 125 basis points of rate hikes despite the risk of hindering already weak growth.
Like other energy importers, the Philippines is vulnerable to supply shocks but it has fewer mechanisms at its disposal to curb fuel prices from spilling over into broader inflation.
A weak peso complicates matters by swelling the country's import bill.

The BSP hasn't shied away from saying it will do what it takes to get inflation under control, leaving the door open to further interest-rates hikes, though some analysts think its tightening cycle is nearing an end.
If sustained, the recent pullback in oil prices could provide some reprieve, though the BSP is also keeping an eye on the risk of the El Nino weather phenomenon causing a food-price shock.
Among the top commodity groups contributing to October's inflation were transport, as well as housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy items, accelerated to 5.4% during the month from a revised 4.8% in September.
Year-to-date headline inflation stood at 5.6%, while the core gauge was at 4.0%.
